name: Maria Lassnig
bioShort: Maria Lassnig (1919–2014) was an Austrian artist known for self-portraits grounded in what she called 'body awareness', depicting only the parts of her body she could physically feel while working. She represented Austria at the 1980 Venice Biennale and received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement in 2013. The NCAI Collection holds a group of her drawings from the 1980s to the 2000s.
bioLong: Maria Lassnig was born in 1919 in Kappel am Krappfeld, Carinthia, Austria, and died in Vienna in 2014. She studied at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna during the Second World War. In 1948 she coined the term Körpergefühlmalerei ('body awareness' or 'body sensation' painting) to describe a practice in which she depicted only the parts of her body she actually felt as she worked, which is why many of her figures are missing body parts or are rendered in unnatural colours.

In 1951 she travelled to Paris with Arnulf Rainer, where she met André Breton and Paul Celan. By the 1960s she had turned away from abstraction to concentrate on the human body and psyche. From 1968 to 1980 she lived in New York, where she studied animated film at the School of Visual Arts and made a series of short films. In 1980 she became professor of painting at the University of Applied Arts Vienna, the first woman to hold such a professorship in a German-speaking country.

Lassnig represented Austria at the Venice Biennale in 1980 and took part in documenta in 1982 and 1997. She was the first woman to receive the Grand Austrian State Prize (1988) and was awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the 2013 Venice Biennale. The NCAI Collection holds a substantial group of her works on paper in pencil, charcoal and pastel, including Cerebralstabilisator / Anatomie von mir (1996) and Die Brüder (c. 1983).
notes: Non-African (Austrian) artist with 23 works on paper in the collection; worth confirming provenance and attribution. Several work titles contain hyphenation artefacts from a PDF/OCR source (e.g. 'Cerebralstabili-sator', 'Nervengeflim-mer'); 'Shooted star' may also need checking. Wikipedia text is inconsistent on when her professorship ended (1997 vs. until her death), so the end date is left out.

name: Sahej Rahal
bioShort: Sahej Rahal (b. 1988, Mumbai) is an Indian artist whose sculptures, films, paintings, installations, video games and AI simulations build counter-mythologies drawn from folklore, science fiction and hidden histories. He has exhibited at the Gwangju, Liverpool and Kochi-Muziris biennales and teaches at UCLA. The NCAI Collection holds sculpture, drawings and software-based works by him from 2018 to 2024.
bioLong: Sahej Rahal was born in Mumbai in 1988 and graduated in painting from the Rachana Sansad Academy of Fine Arts and Crafts, Mumbai, in 2011. He is an assistant professor in the Department of Design Media Arts at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Rahal describes himself as a storyteller who weaves counter-mythologies that question narrations of the present. Drawing characters from sources ranging from local legends and occult manuscripts to archaeological conspiracies and science fiction, he gives this myth world form across sculpture, performance, film, painting, installation, video games and AI simulation programs. A self-taught game programmer, he made the multiplayer game Distributed Mind Test, shown at the 2024 Biennial of Moving Images in Geneva.

His work has been shown at the Kochi-Muziris Biennale and Vancouver Biennale (2014), the Liverpool Biennial and Setouchi Triennale (2016), the Gwangju Biennale, MACRO in Rome and Gasworks in London. He has received the Inlaks Fine Arts Award (2012) and fellowships including the Henry Moore Fellowship, Akademie Schloss Solitude and the 2024 Eyebeam Democracy Machine Fellowship. The NCAI Collection holds works including Anhad (the Unscalable) (2023), an interactive AI simulation, and sculptures in expanding foam, fur and wood (2024).
notes: Non-African (Indian) artist with 13 works in the collection. Work title 'DMT (DMT (Distributed Mind Test)' is malformed in the CMS; it should probably read 'DMT (Distributed Mind Test)'.

name: Elias Mung'ora
bioShort: Elias Mung'ora (b. 1992, Nyeri) is a Nairobi-based Kenyan artist whose layered canvases combine image transfer, paint and drawing to examine urban space, memory and the traces of earlier histories. He won the Manjano Art Prize in 2016 and is a member of the Brush-Tu Artist Collective. His work was shown at NCAI in Common Ground.
bioLong: Elias Mung'ora was born in Nyeri, Kenya, in 1992 and lives and works in Nairobi. He moved to the city to study for a degree in Real Estate and Property Management before turning to visual art. He is a member of Brush-Tu, a Nairobi artists' collective.

Mung'ora is a close observer of lived spaces and the memories they hold. Drawing on everyday life in Nairobi and on occasions such as weddings and portrait sessions, his work looks at urban fragmentation and at how imbalances in physical space affect the people who live in it. He works across painting, drawing, photography and woodcut, building canvases in which image transfers carrying historical references sit alongside expressive brushwork and detailed figures. Works in the NCAI Collection, such as Footprints (2017) and In Between Spaces II (Buroti Maguta Maguta) (2023), combine acrylic with photo and image transfer; the Cleanliness is Next to Godliness series (2024) extends this into screen printing, ballpoint and soap.

He won the Manjano Art Prize in Nairobi in 2016 and was a top-ten finalist in the Barclays L'Atelier competition. His exhibitions include a solo show, Journal Entries, at the Little Art Gallery (2016), group shows at Circle Art Gallery and the British Institute in East Africa, and The Ghost in the Machine at Montague Contemporary (2020). His work was shown at NCAI in Common Ground.
notes: Work title '50 by 100(Buroti Maguta Maguta' is malformed in the CMS (missing closing parenthesis). Sources disagree on the Barclays L'Atelier finalist year (2017 vs 2018), so the year is left out.

name: Sandra Wauye
bioShort: Sandra Wauye (b. 1996) is a Kenyan painter and ceramicist based in Mombasa. Trained as a civil engineer, she turned to art and now addresses grief and trauma processing at the intersection of community, cultural practice and healing ritual. In 2024 she took part in UJUZI, the NCAI and Untethered Magic research and mentorship programme, which ended in an exhibition at NCAI.
bioLong: Sandra Wauye was born in 1996 and lives and works in Mombasa, Kenya. She trained and worked as a civil engineer before becoming a visual artist, and taught herself oil painting and gouache illustration.

Her practice, in painting and clay, deals with grief and trauma processing at the intersection of community, cultural practices and healing rituals. Her paintings set human and animal forms against vibrant, multi-coloured and undefined environments, combining bold colour applied in thick, loose strokes with thinner, controlled outlines in oil and oil pastel stick. Works in the NCAI Collection, all from 2024, include the oil and chalk paintings Collectively Composting and Does The Mold Ever Break? and the clay works Sanctum of Order and Sanctum of Chaos.

Wauye was an artist in residence at 32° East in Kampala in 2023 and took part in the 2024 KLA ART Festival, themed Care Instructions. In 2024 she joined UJUZI, an artistic research and mentorship programme run by the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute and Untethered Magic, which ended in an exhibition at NCAI. Earlier exhibitions include the National Museums of Kenya Affordable Art Show and the Pink Flame exhibition of emerging women artists (both 2022), and in 2025 she showed in New Visions at Circle Art Gallery.
notes: The CMS lists no NCAI exhibitions, but Circle Art Agency says she took part in the 2024 UJUZI programme, which ended in an exhibition at NCAI. Consider linking that exhibition.

name: Jackson Wanjau
bioShort: Jackson Wanjau (b. 1966) is a Kenyan sculptor working in wood and stone. The son of the sculptor Samuel Wanjau, he trained as a primary school teacher and worked alongside his father before turning to sculpture full time in 1994. The NCAI Collection holds four of his wood carvings of everyday and family scenes, from 1997 and 2005.
bioLong: Jackson Wanjau was born in Kenya in 1966. He is the son of the Kenyan sculptor Samuel Wanjau. At first he chose not to follow his father's path and trained as a primary school teacher, but he worked alongside his father in his spare time and committed to sculpture full time in 1994.

Working in wood and stone, Wanjau reveals figures, animals and narratives from the material in a way that shows his father's influence, while giving his forms their own character through angles, distortion and careful finishing and detail.

The NCAI Collection holds four wood carvings by Wanjau whose subjects are drawn from everyday life and family relationships: Street Beggar, Man Drinking Porridge and Lift Me Up Mummy (all 1997), and Loving Mother The Kiss (2005). His work has also been offered at Art Auction East Africa in Nairobi, including the wood carving Hornbills (1998), and he is listed among the sculptors represented by the Mbari Institute for Contemporary African Art.
notes: Mbari Institute gives the father's name as 'Samuel Jackson', most likely an error for Samuel Wanjau. Not the same person as Anthony Wanjau (b. 1971), who also comes from the Wanjau family of sculptors.

name: Sam Ntiro
bioShort: Sam Joseph Ntiro (1923–1993) was a Tanzanian painter and educator who studied at Makerere College and the Slade School of Fine Art and became Professor of Painting at Makerere. He painted daily life in the Chagga country of Kilimanjaro, and in 1960 became the first African artist to enter the collection of the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
bioLong: Sam Joseph Ntiro was born in 1923 in Ndereny village, Machame, in the Kilimanjaro region of what is now Tanzania, and died in 1993. He went to school in Moshi and studied at Makerere College in Kampala from 1944 to 1947, where he first received formal art training. After graduating he was employed by Margaret Trowell to teach painting at Makerere, and he later did postgraduate study at the Slade School of Fine Art in London, graduating in 1955 and returning to Makerere, where he became Professor of Painting.

In 1961 Ntiro left Makerere to become Tanganyika's first High Commissioner to the Court of St James's in London, serving until 1964. He later taught at the University of Dar es Salaam as resident artist, senior lecturer and associate professor.

Working in oil with loose, swirling brushstrokes, Ntiro painted the landscape and life of Chagga country on the southern slopes of Kilimanjaro: banana beer ceremonies, cattle, agricultural labour and village gatherings. In 1960 he became the first African artist to enter the collection of the Museum of Modern Art, New York. His work is also held by the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art and The Phillips Collection. NCAI's works by Ntiro include Agony in the Garden (1950), and in 2026 NCAI showed his work at the 61st Venice Biennale alongside other Makerere-trained artists.
notes: Canonical full name is Sam Joseph Ntiro; 'Sam Ntiro' is the common short form. Three of the four works are undated in the CMS.

name: Kivuthi Mbuno
bioShort: Kivuthi Mbuno (1947–2026) was a self-taught Kenyan artist whose precise drawings in coloured pencil, crayon and pastel drew on Kamba culture and the wildlife he encountered as a safari cook. Promoted by Ruth Schaffner at Gallery Watatu, he showed internationally, including at Africa Explores (1991), and represented Kenya at the 2013 Venice Biennale.
bioLong: Kivuthi Mbuno was born in 1947 in Mwangini, Machakos District, Kenya, and died in 2026. Before becoming an artist he worked as a cook on safaris through the national parks and interior of Kenya and Tanzania. In 1976 he settled in Langata, outside Nairobi, and devoted himself to drawing. He was one of the self-taught pioneers of East African modern art and came to prominence in the 1980s and 1990s through Ruth Schaffner's support at Gallery Watatu in Nairobi.

Working in ink, coloured pencil, crayon and pastel, Mbuno brought together animals, people and objects of traditional life within vast open spaces. His style was precise and brightly coloured, and his interpretation of nature, people and animals has been described as strange and almost surreal. Drawing on Kamba mythology, he built a personal visual vocabulary that stayed largely consistent over the years. The NCAI Collection holds three crayon drawings: Food is Life and The Joy of Loving (both 1985) and People Long Ago (1992).

His work was included in Africa Now at the Saatchi Collection, London (1990), Africa Explores: 20th Century African Art in New York (1991) and, more recently, When We See Us (2022–25). He was selected to represent Kenya at the 55th Venice Biennale in 2013. His work is held by the Contemporary African Art Collection (CAAC), among other collections.
notes: Died 2026, per africancontemporary.com, indigoarts.com and memorial posts on Instagram. Indigo Arts says October 2026; no exact date was confirmed, so the bio uses past tense. Red Hill describes his Kamba community as being in south-eastern Kenya, while CAAC places him in Langata. Red Hill also lists Tate Modern, Dallas and other museum holdings, which were not independently verified and are left out.

name: Dennis Muraguri
bioShort: Dennis Muraguri (b. 1980) is a Kenyan printmaker and sculptor based at the Kuona Artists' Collective in Nairobi. He is known for energetic woodcut prints of matatus, Nairobi's privately run minibuses, which record their names, graffiti and sound-system culture as part of the city's informal transport economy. He showed at the Kochi-Muziris Biennale in 2018.
bioLong: Dennis Muraguri was born in Kenya in 1980 and received a diploma in painting and art history from the Buruburu Institute of Fine Art in 2003. He has been a resident artist at the Kuona Artists' Collective in Nairobi since 2007, working mainly in printmaking and sculpture.

Muraguri is best known for woodcut prints of matatu culture. The matatus he depicts, privately run minibuses that serve as Nairobi's main public transport, are elaborately customised with large sound systems, screens, Wi-Fi and graffiti and collage. In picturing them, he captures what has been called 'the social interstices created by the explosive creativity in the unregulated transport economy of Kenya'. Each print gives a particular vehicle its personality, often naming it as the matatus themselves do. Both works in the NCAI Collection are woodcut prints on paper titled after matatu saccos: Krook 1 Umoinner Sacco (2020) and Matatu Kacose Sacco (2024).

His exhibitions include shows at Circle Art Gallery, Nairobi (2016) and a solo exhibition at Montague Contemporary, New York (2020). Jua Kali (2014), a collaborative installation, was later included in Making Africa: A Continent of Contemporary Design at the Vitra Design Museum (2015). He has shown at the KLA Public Art Festival in Kampala (2014), 1:54 London and the Joburg Art Fair (2016), and was a selected artist at the 2018 Kochi-Muziris Biennale.
notes: Work title 'Krook 1 Umoinner Sacco' may be a transcription of matatu lettering; worth checking against the print.

name: Chain Muhandi
bioShort: Chain Muhandi (b. 1957, Ngecha, Limuru) is a Kenyan painter and one of the founders of the Ngecha artists' community outside Nairobi. He began as a batik artist, was mentored by Ruth Schaffner of Gallery Watatu, and makes narrative paintings of political and social commentary drawn from real events, such as Life in Prison (1994) in the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Chain Muhandi was born Charles Ng'ang'a Kuria in 1957 in Ngecha village, Limuru, Kiambu County, Kenya. He started out making batik and was mentored by Ruth Schaffner of Gallery Watatu, through whom he took part in exhibitions and workshops. He is one of the founders of the Ngecha artists' community on the outskirts of Nairobi, which has produced many of the country's self-taught painters. In 1995 he co-founded the Ngecha Artists Association with artists including Wanyu Brush, Sane Wadu, King Dodge and Meek Gichugu. He later worked for a time at Kuona Trust.

Muhandi's paintings are narrative and often draw on real events to comment on politics and society. Working in gouache, acrylic and natural pigments that he mixes in his studio, he aims to speak directly to viewers about injustice, reflecting his belief that art can educate and uplift society. The NCAI Collection holds Life in Prison (1994, oil on canvas) and Taxi (1997, acrylic on canvas).

He has had three extended residencies in Germany and has exhibited in Europe, Asia and the United States, as well as in Nairobi at venues including the Goethe-Institut, the French Cultural Centre and the Kenya Art Panorama.
notes: Birth name Charles Ng'ang'a Kuria. The biographical detail comes mainly from an auction catalogue and a sales-platform bio (Veno.Art).

name: Francis Kahuri
bioShort: Francis Kahuri (b. 1947) is a Kenyan painter of the generation promoted by Gallery Watatu. He first made his name in batik, later learned oil painting through the Kenya Art Society, and depicts Agikuyu oral history, folk tales and community life in flattened, distorted forms against textured grounds. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Francis Kahuri was born in Kenya in 1947 and belongs to an important generation of Kenyan artists. He worked in insurance until he discovered batik through a neighbour, and his batiks sold well enough that he left his job to pursue art full time. It was with batik that he first exhibited internationally. A meeting with the artist Elimo Njau broadened his artistic horizons, and through the Kenya Art Society he learned to paint in oils.

Because materials were expensive, Kahuri kept working mainly in batik until 1984, when Ruth Schaffner of Gallery Watatu took him on as one of her artists and encouraged him to concentrate on painting. This began the second phase of his career.

Kahuri's work draws on the cultural practices, stories and oral history of the Agikuyu. He paints scenes of domestic life and of the mutual support a community provides, an idyll of simple traditional culture rendered in flattened, somewhat distorted forms against textured backgrounds. His paintings have been shown in Nairobi, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, the United States and Japan. The NCAI Collection holds Fruit Sellers and Double Vision / Oneness (both 1997, acrylic on canvas), and his work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Birth year conflict: Artsy and the Smithsonian Libraries artist file give 1947; an Art Auction East Africa 2023 lot gives 1946. 1947 is used.

name: Elimo Njau
bioShort: Elimo Njau (b. 1932) is a Tanzanian-born painter, sculptor and educator trained at Makerere, and a central figure in modern art in Kenya. In 1959 he painted murals of the life of Christ for the cathedral in Murang'a, and in 1965 he founded Paa ya Paa Arts Centre in Nairobi with Phillda Njau. His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho.
bioLong: Elimo Njau was born in Tanzania in 1932 and studied fine art at the Margaret Trowell School of Fine Art at Makerere in Uganda. Although Tanzanian by birth and trained in Uganda, he is best known for his contribution to art in Kenya, and his life and work have been described as an example of movement across East Africa.

In 1959 he painted five murals at St James and All Martyrs Cathedral in Murang'a (formerly Fort Hall), Kenya, as a memorial to those who died during the Mau Mau uprising. They depict the Nativity, the Baptism, the Last Supper, the Agony in the Garden and the Crucifixion.

In the early 1960s Njau worked with writers and intellectuals including Ezekiel Mphahlele, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Okot p'Bitek and Jonathan Kariara, and led the visual arts programme at the Chemchemi Cultural Centre in Nairobi. In 1965 he and his wife, Phillda Njau, founded the Paa ya Paa Arts Centre in Nairobi, whose name means 'the antelope rises'. After a fire damaged the premises in 1997, it was rebuilt as an open-air gallery.
The NCAI Collection holds Dream Landscape (1968, oil on canvas). His work was shown at NCAI in Mwili, Akili Na Roho, and NCAI presented an artist portrait film about him at the 2026 Venice Biennale.
notes: Living status was not confirmed beyond 'b. 1932' in early-2026 posts, so the bio uses present tense; check before publishing. Kibos Art Centre (1964) and a Makerere lectureship (1959–62) appear in weaker sources and are left out. The Chemchemi details come mainly from a blog and search summaries; Paa ya Paa (1965) and the Murang'a murals are corroborated.

name: Araba Opoku
bioShort: Araba Opoku (b. 1998, Accra) is a Ghanaian multidisciplinary artist known for large, fluid abstract paintings that address socio-economic issues in Ghana, especially water scarcity and rationing in Accra, as well as mental health and stigma. In 2021 she won the inaugural Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize from Gallery 1957. The NCAI Collection holds Growing Pains (2025).
bioLong: Araba Opoku was born in Accra, Ghana, in 1998 and lives and works there. She studied psychology at the University of Ghana while keeping up her art practice.

Opoku is known for dreamlike abstract paintings of fluid shapes, flowing lines and blended colour, often with repeating, textile-like patterns. She begins each work digitally before moving to canvas, applying acrylic in flowing strokes and letting the paint drip, then restraining that movement with curved grid lines. Her work addresses socio-economic crises in Ghana, especially water scarcity and rationing in Accra, holding together the freedom, joy and abundance that water represents and the hardship caused by its absence. She also takes up mental health and the stigma attached to it. Her paintings refer to her immediate surroundings: particular streets, gardens and scenes of community life.

In 2021 Opoku received the inaugural Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize from Gallery 1957. Her exhibitions include the solo shows Come Hell or High Water at ADA Contemporary Art Gallery, Accra, and Whispers Down the Lane at Gallery 1957 (2022), as well as presentations at ART X Lagos (2021) and EXPO Chicago (2023). The NCAI Collection holds Growing Pains (2025, acrylic on canvas and acrylic on wood).
notes: Non-East-African (Ghanaian) artist. Her full name per her Instagram is Maame Araba Baboa Opoku.

name: Selasi Sosu
bioShort: Selasi Awusi Sosu (b. 1976, Kumasi) is a Ghanaian artist, educator and researcher who works with glass, sound and video. She represented Ghana in the country's first pavilion at the 58th Venice Biennale (2019). Her glass tablet Incising Nkrumah into Our Present (2023), in the NCAI Collection, was shown at the 35th Ljubljana Biennale of Graphic Arts.
bioLong: Selasi Awusi Sosu was born in Kumasi, Ghana, in 1976 and lives and works in Accra and Winneba. She studied textiles at Achimota School and completed bachelor's and master's degrees in fine art, in sculpture, at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, where she later began doctoral research. She has taught art in Kumasi and teaches at the University of Education, Winneba.

Glass is central to her practice. For Ghana's first national pavilion at the 58th Venice Biennale in 2019, she presented work about an abandoned glass factory in Ghana, using glass alongside photography, video and sound to celebrate the beauty of the material and to criticise the decay and mismanagement of the site.

Her recent work examines labour in urban Ghana through installations that engage several senses. She records the chants, songs, prayers, shouts and cries of informal-sector workers on the streets of Accra, Winneba and other cities, and reflects on the sounds and physical traces left in abandoned post-independence factories such as the Tarkwa glass factory. At the 35th Ljubljana Biennale of Graphic Arts she showed The Songs of Labour and Nkruumah brebereee, one cedi' alongside Incising Nkrumah into Our Present (2023), a glass tablet inscribed with references to Kwame Nkrumah. That work is now in the NCAI Collection.
notes: Non-East-African (Ghanaian) artist. CMS name 'Selasi Sosu' omits her middle name; she is professionally credited as Selasi Awusi Sosu. Status of the doctorate (begun at KNUST in 2008) is unconfirmed.

name: Rebecca Bisaso
bioShort: Rebecca Bisaso is a Ugandan painter represented in the NCAI Collection by Woman's Burden (1990, oil on board). The painting addresses armed conflict and the AIDS epidemic that affected Ugandan society in the 1980s. It was formerly in the collection of Robert Loder, co-founder of the Triangle network, and was shown in Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa at the Whitechapel Gallery in 1995.
bioLong: Rebecca Bisaso is a Ugandan artist. Little published biographical information about her is available, and she is known mainly through a single painting, Woman's Burden (1990, oil on board), now in the NCAI Collection.

The painting comes from a period when Ugandan society was dealing with both political conflict and the AIDS epidemic. In a survey of modern art in Uganda, the Eastern African Modern Art Network notes that in this work Bisaso 'addresses the connected issues of armed conflict and the ravages of the disease' during the 1980s.

Woman's Burden measures 122 by 64 centimetres. It was acquired in 1993 by Robert Loder (1934–2017), the British collector and co-founder of the Triangle network of artists' workshops. While in his collection, it was shown in Seven Stories about Modern Art in Africa at the Whitechapel Gallery, London, in 1995, where Uganda was represented by artists including Bisaso, C. Driciru, Pilkington Ssengendo and Ignatius Sserulyo. The painting has since entered the NCAI Collection, where it is one of a number of works that trace modern painting in Uganda.
notes: Biography unknown; the bio is built around the single work. The EAMAN text gives the title as 'Woman of Burden', the Loder catalogue and CMS as 'Woman's Burden'. A Daily Monitor article (2024) describes a Rebecca Bisaso retiring as a teacher after 31 years (career from 1993); not confirmed to be the same person, so not used. The Loder/Whitechapel provenance suggests this work came to NCAI via the Robert Loder Collection. The list of Ugandan artists in Seven Stories comes from a 32° East Facebook post seen only as a search excerpt.

name: Chang
bioShort: Chang is an artist recorded as Ugandan, represented in the NCAI Collection by Talking Tree, a painting in oil on board. The work was formerly in the collection of Robert Loder, co-founder of the Triangle network of artists' workshops, whose catalogue dates it to 1993 and lists it under a working title. No further biographical information has been confirmed.
bioLong: Chang is an artist recorded as Ugandan, known by a single name. No published biography has been found, and the artist is known through one painting, Talking Tree, in oil on board, now in the NCAI Collection.

The painting was formerly in the collection of Robert Loder (1934–2017), the British collector and co-founder of the Triangle network of international artists' workshops. The catalogue of his collection lists it as Talking Tree (Working Title), oil on board, about 109 by 140 centimetres, made and acquired in 1993. The note 'working title' suggests the name may have been assigned when it was catalogued rather than given by the artist.

The work belongs to a group of paintings by Ugandan artists from the late 1980s and early 1990s that Loder collected, several of which are now in the NCAI Collection. Further research into the artist's full name, training and wider practice is needed before more can be said.
notes: Single-name artist with no biography found. The Loder Collection gives a date of 1993 and the country as Uganda, while the CMS lists the work as 'Undated'; consider updating to 1993. The title is a working title. 'Several of which are now in the NCAI Collection' is inferred from this batch (Bisaso, Chang, Akobo all trace to Loder); verify.

name: David Koloane
bioShort: David Koloane (1938–2019) was a South African artist, writer, curator and teacher who worked to open space for Black artists during and after apartheid, co-founding the Thupelo workshop and the Bag Factory Artists' Studios. His expressive paintings and drawings of Johannesburg include the Street Dogs series. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: David Koloane was born in 1938 in Alexandra, Johannesburg, and died in 2019. He worked as an artist, writer, curator, teacher and mentor at a time when such roles were largely closed to Black South Africans. He helped establish the first Black Art Gallery in 1977, the Thupelo experimental workshop in 1985 and the Bag Factory Artists' Studios in 1991, which he directed for many years. He tutored at the Federated Union of Black Artists (FUBA) from 1979 and headed its fine art section and gallery from 1985 to 1990.

Koloane made Johannesburg his main subject, examining social, political and existential conditions through cityscapes, townships, street life, jazz musicians, traffic, migration, and the dogs and birds that recur in his work. Working in painting, drawing, collage, printmaking and mixed media, he made scenes that range between the exuberant and the sombre. Street Dogs 10 (2005, acrylic and pastel on paper), in the NCAI Collection, belongs to his series on the city's stray dogs.

His work was included in Liberated Voices at the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art (1999) and in the South African Pavilion at the 55th Venice Biennale (2013). He received a Prince Claus Award in 1998 and honorary doctorates from the University of the Witwatersrand (2012) and Rhodes University (2015). His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Non-East-African (South African) artist.

name: Wairimũ Nduba
bioShort: Wairimũ Nduba is a Kenyan multidisciplinary creative, researcher and curator whose practice is guided by African sonic principles that treat music as a site of community and healing. She founded Wer Jokenya, a digital archive of Kenya's music histories, and draws on a long background in ballet. The NCAI Collection holds her sound installation Can You Hold A Sound (2025).
bioLong: Wairimũ Nduba is a Kenyan multidisciplinary creative whose practice is rooted in, and guided by, African sonic principles that understand music as a site of community and healing. She works mainly through research, music history and curation, and her work centres on how sound shapes community and memory.

Her practice combines sonic-visual archiving with curation. She founded Wer Jokenya, a digital archival platform documenting the breadth of Kenya's music history and the social and political dimensions carried within it. Through the platform she treats recorded and remembered music as a living archive and a way into histories that written records often leave out.

Nduba also has an 18-year background in ballet, first as a dancer and then as a teacher. She uses this experience to explore how the body works as an archive, particularly within African practices of embodied knowledge. Her work moves between music, movement and sonic-visual research. The NCAI Collection holds her sound installation Can You Hold A Sound (2025).
notes: Primarily a researcher, curator and archivist rather than a conventional studio artist. Birth year not found.

name: Charles Mukiibi
bioShort: Charles Mukiibi is a painter who trained at Makerere University in Kampala and is represented in the NCAI Collection by The Arrest (1966, oil on canvas). His work was included in The Early Years, an exhibition of early paintings at the Makerere Art Gallery in 2011, and NCAI showed The Arrest at the 61st Venice Biennale in 2026.
bioLong: Charles Mukiibi is a painter who trained at Makerere University in Kampala, the art school founded by Margaret Trowell that shaped several generations of East African modernists. Little further biographical information about him has been published.

The NCAI Collection holds The Arrest (1966), an oil on canvas measuring 84 by 61 centimetres. It belongs to the period of the 1960s when Makerere-trained painters were taking up figurative subjects drawn from everyday and social life in post-independence East Africa. Another painting by Mukiibi, Dispensary, was included in The Early Years, an exhibition of early works at the Makerere Art Gallery in 2011.

In 2026 the Nairobi Contemporary Art Institute was an invited participant at the 61st Venice Biennale. It presented eight works from its collection made between 1950 and 1984 by artists trained at Makerere: Sam Ntiro, Charles Mukiibi, Kefa Ssempangi, C. Driciru, Josephine Alacu, Peter Mulindwa and Godfrey Banadda. The Arrest was among them.
notes: Nationality assumed Ugandan from Makerere context; not explicitly confirmed by a source. Not to be confused with the self-taught Ugandan painter Enoch Mukiibi. The Early Years / Dispensary detail comes from a Start Journal search excerpt (the page itself returned a server error). The Arrest's dimensions come from NCAI's own Instagram caption. 'The Arrest was among them' is inferred from NCAI Instagram posts listing The Arrest with the Venice presentation; check against NCAI records. The line about 1960s figurative subjects is context, not sourced; cut it if unwanted.

name: Maame Adjoa Ohemeng
bioShort: Maame Adjoa Ohemeng (b. 2000) is a Ghanaian painter based in Accra who trained at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. Her mixed-media paintings build surreal, fragmented scenes in which hybrid characters, part real and part virtual, explore identity, relationships and everyday ritual, often through women's stories. She was a runner-up for Gallery 1957's Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.
bioLong: Maame Adjoa Ohemeng was born in 2000 and is a Ghanaian visual artist based in Accra. She trained in painting at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi and is part of blaxTARLINES, the project space and community for emerging artists linked to the KNUST art school.

Working in painting and mixed media, Ohemeng combines figurative imagery with decorative surfaces to make surreal, fragmented compositions. In her words, the work 'constructs surreal, fragmented scenes where hybrid characters—part real, part virtual—explore identity, relationships and everyday rituals'. She builds illusionistic depth that pushes past the edge of the canvas, a layered 'ordered chaos'. Her subjects centre on women's stories, friendship and contemporary life in Ghana: through portraiture and invented narratives, she looks at how personal history and cultural identity shape the lives of young women moving between tradition and modernity.

Ohemeng was a runner-up for Gallery 1957's Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize and has shown in group exhibitions in Ghana, Kenya and Italy. The NCAI Collection holds What Will This Holy Grail Dominant Painting (2024), made with oil paint, acrylic and plaster of Paris.
notes: Non-East-African (Ghanaian) artist. The work title 'What Will This Holy Grail Dominant Painting' looks truncated or garbled; check it with the artist or the acquisition record. 'Ordered chaos' and the edge of the canvas come from an Instagram post seen only as a search excerpt.

name: Afewerk Tekle
bioShort: Afewerk Tekle (1932–2012) was an Ethiopian painter and stained-glass artist known for work on African and Christian themes, including the stained-glass windows of Africa Hall in Addis Ababa. Trained in London at the Central School of Arts and Crafts and the Slade, he was the first laureate of the Haile Selassie I Prize for Fine Arts. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Afewerk Tekle was born on 22 October 1932 in Ankober, Shewa, Ethiopia, and died in Addis Ababa on 10 April 2012. He went to Britain intending to study mining engineering but instead studied painting, sculpture and architecture at the Central School of Arts and Crafts and the Slade School of Fine Art in London.

He became known for paintings on African and Christian themes and for his stained glass, and his work engaged with Black emancipation and the struggles for African independence. His major works include the three stained-glass windows of Total Liberation of Africa (1958), covering about 150 square metres in Africa Hall, Addis Ababa; the painting Maskal Flower (1961); the mural The Last Judgment (1970) in Adigrat Cathedral; and the Ras Makonnen monument in Harar.

In 1964 Afewerk was the first laureate of the Haile Selassie I Prize for Fine Arts. In 1981 his self-portrait became the first work by an African artist to enter the permanent collection of the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, and in 1983 he became the first African member of the Russian Academy of Arts. The NCAI Collection holds Afar Boy (1974, gouache on paper), and his work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Ethiopian. Some sources style him 'Maitre Artiste Afewerk Tekle'. Ethiopian naming convention: the short form is 'Afewerk', not 'Tekle'.

name: Akobo
bioShort: Akobo is an artist known by a single name, represented in the NCAI Collection by Headless Belly Dancer, an undated painting in oil on board. The work was formerly in the collection of Robert Loder, co-founder of the Triangle network of artists' workshops, where it is listed under a working title. No further biographical information has been confirmed.
bioLong: Akobo is an artist recorded under a single name. No published biography has been found, and the artist's nationality, dates and training are unknown. Akobo is known through one painting in the NCAI Collection, Headless Belly Dancer, an undated work in oil on board.

The painting was formerly in the collection of Robert Loder (1934–2017), the British collector and co-founder of the Triangle network of international artists' workshops, whose holdings documented contemporary art from across Africa and beyond. The online catalogue of his collection lists the work as Headless Belly Dancer (Working Title) but gives no date, medium or country. The note 'working title' suggests the name may have been assigned when the work was catalogued rather than chosen by the artist.

Several works that Loder collected, including paintings in oil on board by East African artists, have since entered the NCAI Collection. Further research, for example in Loder's records or the archives of the Triangle workshops, is needed to establish who Akobo was and where the work was made.
notes: Single-name artist; nationality unknown, so it is set to null. 'Akobo' is also a place name in South Sudan and Ethiopia, possibly a lead. The title is a working title per the Loder Collection. 'Including paintings ... by East African artists' is inferred from this batch (Bisaso, Chang); verify.

name: Gakunju Kaigwa
bioShort: Gakunju Kaigwa (b. 1958) is a Kenyan sculptor who works in stone, wood, glass, steel, bronze and resin. Trained in fine art at Kenyatta University, in Carrara and at the University of Dundee, he has made public sculpture in Kenya and abroad and has a studio at the Kuona Trust in Nairobi. His work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
bioLong: Gakunju Kaigwa was born in Kenya in 1958. He studied at Lenana School and graduated from Kenyatta University with a Bachelor of Education in Fine Art in 1980. He trained first as a painter and worked in design for Voice of Kenya television before turning to sculpture in the early 1980s.

In 1988 he received a scholarship to study at the Accademia di Belle Arti in Carrara, Italy. He completed a master's degree in Public Art at the University of Dundee, Scotland, in 1993, and then trained at the Johnson Atelier Technical Institute of Sculpture in New Jersey, where he learned foundry work and metal casting. After working in the United States, he returned to Kenya in 2003 and set up his studio at the Kuona Trust Centre for Visual Arts in Nairobi, where he takes public and private commissions.

Kaigwa is known for his command of many materials, including wood, glass, steel, bronze, granite, marble, resin and stone, and his sculptures stand in public spaces in Kenya and abroad. He also works as a musician and actor. The NCAI Collection holds Chai Moto (1990), a carving in Kisii soapstone, and his work was shown at NCAI in 60 Years: the NCAI Collection.
notes: Art Auction East Africa 2023 sold 'Chai Motto' (1990, Kisii soapstone, signed 'B.G KAIGWA 1990'), probably the same work as NCAI's 'Chai Moto'; the spelling differs. The degree is called an MFA by the auction house and a 'Master's degree in Public Art' by Debunk. The Business Daily source was seen only as a search excerpt.
